title: Eval & Regression Monitoring Workshop - Pendulum Health
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a hands-on walkthrough of Console evaluation features (prompt sets, regression alerts, A/B comparison dashboard, and API eval endpoints). Pendulum is evaluating quality monitoring for their clinical triage assistant; key concerns were data residency, false positive regression alerts and latency vs cost tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: sandbox access, shared eval template, schedule POC scoping call.

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-04-12 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 57 minutes
- Attendees: Aisha Patel, Miguel Santos (Redwood); Dana Kim, Ravi Menon, Sofia Alvarez (Pendulum Health)

[00:00] Aisha: ok hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Aisha from Redwood Inference. real quick, can we just do a 30-second roll call?
[00:10] Dana: hi this is Dana, head of ML at Pendulum.
[00:13] Ravi: Ravi here, platform eng.
[00:15] Sofia: Sofia from product.
[00:18] Miguel: Miguel, solutions engineer, I'll run the demo with Aisha.
[00:22] Aisha: great. Today we'll walk through Eval in the console — prompt sets, regression alerting, and the A over B comparison flows. We'll also touch on the API endpoints if you want to run automated evals. If at any point interrupt, please.
[00:33] Dana: sounds good. our use case is clinical triage chat — very sensitive. We want reliable quality monitoring and quick regression detection when models or prompts change.
[00:41] Aisha: understood. And what's your primary deployment target? hosted api or private?
[00:46] Ravi: ideally private VPC but for the POC we're okay with hosted sandbox. main gating is data residency and encryption at rest.
[00:52] Miguel: noted. we have KMS options and on-prem packaging, plus audit logs for every eval run. I'll point to the security packet at the end.
[00:58] [00:58] Miguel: okay sharing screen — give me a sec. (screen share starts)
[01:05] Miguel: this is the Redwood Console Eval tab. top-left is Prompt Sets. you can create a set by uploading CSV/JSONL or link a test-suite in our eval-template. here we have an example 'clinical-triage-50' with intents, reference completions, and metadata tags.
[01:22] Sofia: that CSV schema — does it support structured fields? like symptom severity, patient_age?
[01:27] Miguel: yes, you can have nested JSON payloads in the input column; console will surface those as columns. bear in mind transcription sometimes flattens the schema if fields are similar, i've seen that in exports, but it's there.
[01:38] Dana: how do you define automated checks? precision recall? fuzzy match?
[01:42] Miguel: good question. we have a library of metrics — exact match, BLEU, embedding similarity (cosine), and custom regex or heuristics. you can plug a custom scorer as well via the API for domain-specific metrics.
[01:52] Ravi: what about regression alerts? we need low noise — false positives are costly when clinical flows are impacted.
[01:57] Miguel: the alerting system uses a baseline window and can use percentile thresholds and rolling medians. also you can attach guardrails that require confirmation from two separate metrics before firing an alert. that cut down noise in our internal tests.
[02:10] Aisha: i'll show an example. (click) here's an alert rule "median_similarity_drop" — it fired last week in a demo because a model variant changed quantization. console shows a diff view with top failing prompts, sample model outputs, and suspected root cause.
[02:24] Dana: can we see the A/B compare for those prompts?
[02:27] Miguel: yes, opening the A/B view. this UI shows side-by-side completions, token-level highlight differences, and a scoring delta. you can apply filters — by tag, by cost bucket, or by latency.
[02:38] Sofia: token-level highlights — is that deterministic? our annotators want to know exactly what changed to judge severity.
[02:44] Miguel: it's deterministic for same random seed and same model variant; when we do sampling there will be variability. for eval we recommend deterministic decoding mode (greedy or fixed-topk) to make diffs reproducible.
[02:54] [02:54] (small crosstalk)
[02:56] Dana: can we run evals via API so our CI can block merges on regressions?
[03:00] Miguel: absolutely. we have an /v1/evals/run endpoint — you POST a prompt set id and get back a run id with metrics and per-sample results. we also support webhooks to push alerts into your tooling.
[03:10] Ravi: performance — what kind of latency should we expect for evals? we plan to run 1k samples overnight and some real-time checks.
[03:16] Miguel: batching and caching play a role. for large bulk evals we recommend using dedicated capacity or our batch endpoints which are cheaper. per-sample latency in the hosted mode for a 2k context LLM is around 400–800ms median, but that's model dependent. for nightly jobs batching reduces token egress cost.
[03:32] Dana: any built-in quality for A/B voting? we have annotators, but want automated majority vote plus human review.
[03:38] Aisha: you can configure human-in-the-loop — set a threshold where samples with marginal delta are pushed to an annotation queue. also integration with your labeling tool via S3/CSV export.
[03:47] Sofia: curious about dataset drift detection — do you flag shifts in user intent distributions?
[03:51] Miguel: yes, we do statistical drift detection on prompt metadata and embedding drift using the embeddings from our models or your chosen embedder. flagging triggers are configurable.
[03:58] Ravi: regarding security — are eval payloads retained? can we disable retention for certain datasets?
[04:03] Miguel: retention is configurable per-project. by default sandbox keeps 30 days; for enterprise on private deployment you can set zero retention and route logs to your S3. we support KMS and HSM key wrapping.
[04:14] Dana: ok great. show us a mock regression alert then.
[04:17] Miguel: demoing — here's a run diff where model-v2 produced lower cosine similarity across symptom mapping intents. you can click into the top 10 failing samples, see previous run outputs, and annotate 'false positive' or 'regression'. those annotations update the baseline automatically if you choose.
[04:34] (typing noise)
[04:36] Sofia: the annotation UI looks nice. can we export the failing subset to share with clinical reviewers?
[04:41] Miguel: yes export CSV or push to a labeling queue. exports include context, model outputs, token probs (when available), and trace IDs for debugging. note: token probs might be withheld in some hosted configs for performance.
[04:53] Dana: Aisha, what about in the POC — can we use our own internal models deployed in our VPC and still use Redwood Eval?
[04:59] Aisha: yes. there's a private control plane option where the control plane runs in Redwood but inference calls route to your VPC endpoints, or fully private where both control and runtime is in your environment. for the POC we typically do hosted evals with a tokenized scrubbed dataset, then move to a private eval pass.
[05:15] Ravi: latency vs cost — if we enable continuous eval on production traffic, what's the expected cost impact?
[05:20] Miguel: you can do sampling: route 1% of traffic to full eval with full context, or shadow calls to a cheaper quantized variant. Redwood Optimize helps generate cost-vs-quality curves to pick the sweet spot.
[05:33] Dana: can the system run A/B tests in prod with gradual rollouts?
[05:36] Miguel: yes, there's a rollout policy where you can run canary traffic to model B and automatically divert based on chosen metrics (quality delta, latency, error rate). automatic fallback can route back if quality drops.
[05:46] Sofia: what about labeling guidelines — do you provide recommended rubrics for clinical contexts?
[05:50] Aisha: we have domain-agnostic rubrics and a sample clinical rubric in the eval-template. you'll want to adapt it with your clinical SME. I'll share that doc.
[05:58] (pause)
[06:00] Dana: one thing we worry about: false positives from embedding similarity where synonyms or abbreviations confuse the metric.
[06:07] Miguel: you can use hybrid metrics — combine embedding similarity with token-level heuristics or a clinical intent classifier. many customers create ensembled scorers to reduce noise.
[06:17] Ravi: can you show the API response for an eval run?
[06:20] Miguel: sure. (switches) here is a sample JSON: run_id, metrics {median_cosine: 0.87, delta: -0.12}, per_sample [{prompt_id, prompt_text, model_a, model_b, similarity}]. we redact some fields in the UI for privacy, but API can return full rows for authorized keys.
[06:36] (mis-typed word)
[06:38] Sofia: on the A/B results, can annotators vote and change the winner?
[06:41] Miguel: yes annotators can override and that updates historical metrics if you choose 'apply corrections'. we maintain audit logs for every change.
[06:49] Dana: next for us would be to get the template and a sandbox — and then run a 2-week POC where we push our prompts and collect annotator feedback.
[06:58] Aisha: perfect. we'll provision sandbox access, share the eval-template.xlsx, and propose POC success criteria in the scoping doc.
[07:06] Ravi: any blockers for security review?
[07:09] Aisha: we'll include SOC2 summary, encryption/KMS notes, and an outline of the private deployment options. if you need a full security questionnaire we'll ask our security team to fill it.
[07:18] Dana: ok. can we set the POC perf targets — e.g., median latency under 800ms and threshold of less than 3% critical regressions?
[07:25] Miguel: noted; I'll draft instrumentation for those metrics.
[07:29] (wrap up)
[07:30] Aisha: recap: Redwood shares sandbox and eval-template (Aisha), Miguel drafts POC instrumentation and perf targets (Miguel), Pendulum confirms compliance gating (Ravi). We'll reconvene for scoping.
[07:43] Sofia: thanks all.
[07:45] Dana: thanks.
[07:47] Miguel: thanks, bye.

Notes: transcript contains a few transcription artifacts (e.g., "kay-vee cache" for KV cache; "sam-el" for SAML). References: eval-template.xlsx (shared), console sandbox link (to be provisioned), security_packet_v1.pdf.
